stem: A radiated-emissions measurement is a measurement of:
choices: Electric field strength from the equipment and the cables that leave it
ESD current from a contact tip
explanation: Radiated emissions leave the box and the wiring as a field. Conducted emissions are the voltage on a port, measured with a coupling network.

stem: The Part 15 measurement distance is:
choices: To the centre of the turntable, ignoring cables
Vertical, to the top of the antenna
Horizontal, to the closest point of the system boundary, including support gear and cables
explanation: Section 15.31(f) defines that horizontal distance. A cable that sticks out of the boundary moves the distance.

stem: Above 30 MHz, changing the measurement distance uses:
explanation: Section 15.31(f)(1) uses inverse linear distance, which is 20 dB/decade, at and above 30 MHz. Below 30 MHz the default factor is 40 dB/decade.

stem: A 40 dBµV/m limit at 10 m, moved to 3 m with 20 dB/decade, is about:
explanation: The field is higher at the shorter distance by 20·log10(10/3), about 10.5 dB. 40 dBµV/m at 10 m lines up with about 50 dBµV/m at 3 m.

stem: ICES-002 Table 4 Class B is 40 dBµV/m at 3 m and 30 dBµV/m at 10 m from 30–230 MHz. That 10 dB step is:
choices: A detector change from quasi-peak to average
explanation: 20·log10(10/3) is about 10.5 dB, and the published pair is 40 and 30. The same pattern is 47 and 37 from 230 MHz to 1 GHz.

stem: On and below 1 GHz, the Part 15 radiated limits are based on:
choices: A peak detector with 1 MHz RBW only
explanation: Section 15.35(a) sets quasi-peak at and below 1000 MHz. Peak with the same bandwidth is allowed because it will not under-call the quasi-peak result.

stem: Using a peak detector below 1 GHz, with the quasi-peak bandwidth, is acceptable because:
choices: Peak is always 6 dB lower than quasi-peak
Peak is greater than or equal to quasi-peak, so a passing peak reading passes quasi-peak
explanation: Section 15.35(a) allows that alternative. A failing peak reading does not by itself prove a quasi-peak failure; you still have to measure quasi-peak if you need the margin.

stem: Above 1 GHz, Part 15 and ICES-003 both want:
choices: An average limit and a peak limit, with resolution bandwidth at least 1 MHz
explanation: Section 15.35(b) and ICES-003 Table 4 both use at least 1 MHz bandwidth above 1 GHz. ICES-003 prints 54/74 dBµV/m for Class B and 60/80 for Class A at 3 m.

stem: At 980 MHz the Class B 'above 960 MHz' limit of 500 µV/m is:
explanation: The detector change in §15.35 happens at 1000 MHz, not at 960 MHz. Above 1000 MHz the same 500 µV/m number is read as an average limit.

stem: A maximized radiated scan looks at:
choices: Both antenna polarizations, a turn in azimuth, and the height range the method requires
One cable position chosen for a tidy photo
explanation: The maximum is the number that is compared with the limit. Section 15.31(f)(6) and the usual CISPR 16 / ANSI C63.4 scan exist to find that maximum.

stem: Below 1 GHz on an OATS or SAC, the usual receive-antenna height scan is:
explanation: That 1–4 m scan is standard CISPR 16-2-3 and ANSI C63.4 practice for the 30 MHz to 1 GHz range. Skipping it hides vertically polarized peaks.

stem: Antenna choice by band, in ordinary chamber practice, is:
choices: A rod antenna from 30 MHz to 18 GHz
A LISN as the receiving antenna
A loop for every Class B scan above 1 GHz
Biconical or hybrid low, log-periodic through 1 GHz, and a horn above 1 GHz
explanation: Those are the usual CISPR 16 antennas for the RE ranges. The antenna factor of the antenna you actually used has to be in the result.

stem: A wrong antenna factor:
choices: Shifts every reading in that band by the factor error
Only affects the noise floor display
explanation: The displayed field is receiver voltage plus antenna factor, cable loss, and any preamp gain. A bad factor is a bad result at every frequency where it is applied.

stem: Table-top equipment below 1 GHz is commonly placed at:
explanation: 0.8 m is the long-standing table height in ANSI C63.4 and CISPR 16 practice below 1 GHz. Editions differ in the detail above 1 GHz, so record the height the method you cited actually requires.

stem: The mode used for the final radiated measurement should be:
choices: The intended-use mode that produces the largest emission in the band
A mode the manual says not to use
explanation: EN 301 489-1 clause 8.1.2 and the Part 15 maximize rule both point at the noisiest representative mode. Record which mode that was.

stem: Support equipment and its cables are:
choices: Inside the system boundary and part of what the antenna distance is measured to
Ignored if they are 'just the laptop'
Measured on a second LISN only
explanation: Section 15.31(f) includes support equipment and interconnecting cables in the boundary. A noisy support laptop can be the emission you think is the product.

stem: An open-area site is the Part 15 reference. Another site is usable when:
choices: It is calibrated so the result matches what an OATS would have given
explanation: Section 15.31(d) allows alternative sites only with that correspondence. Site validation (NSA below 1 GHz, site VSWR above 1 GHz) is how CISPR 16-1-4 practice shows the room is fit.

stem: At 30 MHz and a 3 m distance, a careful reading of the setup includes:
choices: The distance is electrically short, so the method and the site validation matter more than a free-space far-field formula
30 MHz is always deep far field at 3 m
Only a loop antenna is legal
explanation: A wavelength at 30 MHz is 10 m, so 3 m is not a comfortable far field. Standards still specify 3 m and require a validated site rather than a textbook far-field correction.

stem: If the ambient is sitting on the limit line, the practical consequence is:
choices: Switch to average and ignore it
Subtract 6 dB and ship the report
You cannot honestly separate the product from the ambient
The product passes because the ambient is 'the environment'
explanation: CISPR 16-2-3 practice treats an ambient that is not comfortably below the limit as a measurement problem, not as a product result. Move the frequency, the time, or the site.

stem: A pre-scan that never turns the table:
choices: Can miss the worst azimuth and is not a final result
explanation: Prescans are a search tool. The reported point is the maximized one, after azimuth, height, polarization, and cable dress.

stem: A saturated preamplifier:
choices: Compresses strong signals and can hide or invent the wrong margin
explanation: If the preamp is in compression, the reading is no longer linear. Check it with a step attenuator when a spur looks suspiciously flat.

stem: Calling a peak reading a quasi-peak pass, with no margin and no quasi-peak remeasure:
choices: Is fine if the peak is under the average limit
Is not a demonstration that the quasi-peak limit is met
explanation: Peak may be used to pass, because it over-reads quasi-peak. A peak reading over the quasi-peak limit does not tell you the quasi-peak result.

stem: The upper frequency of a radiated scan for an unintentional radiator follows:
choices: The highest frequency generated or used, from the §15.33(b)(1) table
explanation: Section 15.33(b)(1) and ICES-003 Table 3 use the same breakpoints: under 1.705 MHz, to 108 MHz, to 500 MHz, to 1 GHz, then five times that frequency capped at 40 GHz.

stem: A digital device whose highest clock is 200 MHz is investigated for radiated emissions up to:
explanation: Both §15.33(b)(1) and ICES-003 Table 3 put 108 MHz < Fx ≤ 500 MHz at an upper frequency of 2 GHz. Stopping at 1 GHz leaves the required range unmeasured.

stem: A device whose highest frequency is 2.4 GHz is investigated up to:
explanation: Above 1 GHz the upper frequency is the fifth harmonic or 40 GHz, whichever is lower. Five times 2.4 GHz is 12 GHz, which is under the cap.

stem: Outdoor satellite-receive units under ICES-003 are measured to:
choices: 18 GHz, and Annex H of CAN/CSA-CISPR 32:17 applies even if ANSI C63.4 is the method
The same FM as any other ITE, with Annex H optional
explanation: Section 3.2.2 sets 18 GHz for those outdoor units and points the limits at Table A.7 of the CISPR 32 adoption. This quiz does not invent the numbers inside that table.

stem: IEC 61000-6-3:2020, in the file this lab uploaded, is:
choices: A preview of the generic residential emission standard, not a full limit table
explanation: The upload is marked as a preview. It shows that Tables 3 to 6 exist for the enclosure, AC mains, DC power, and other wired ports, and it does not reproduce those numbers.

stem: From the IEC 61000-6-3 preview, measurements are performed:
choices: Only on ports the equipment actually has
On every port in the standard, even if the product has no cable there
explanation: The preview says measurements are carried out where the relevant ports exist, and the test plan still has to consider every applicable row.

stem: CISPR 14-1, from the preview's title and contents, applies to:
choices: Household appliances, electric tools, and similar apparatus, and it distinguishes continuous from discontinuous disturbances
explanation: The preview's title and contents list that product family, continuous disturbances, and discontinuous disturbances (clicks). The preview is not the numeric limit tables.
citation: EN IEC 55014-1:2021 preview, title and contents

stem: Class B under §15.109(a) at 3 m, 30–88 MHz, is:
explanation: That is the first row of the Class B table, specified at 3 m. Do not paste the Class A 10 m number into a 3 m report.

stem: Class B under §15.109(a) at 3 m, above 960 MHz, is:
explanation: The above-960 MHz Class B row is 500 µV/m at 3 m. Above 1 GHz, §15.35 reads that limit as an average limit with a peak cap 20 dB higher.

stem: Class A radiated limits in §15.109(b) are specified at:
explanation: The Class A table is a 10 m table: 90, 150, 210, and 300 µV/m across the four bands. Quoting it at 3 m without the 20 dB/decade move is a different limit.

stem: ICES-003 Class B quasi-peak at 3 m from 230 MHz to 960 MHz is:
explanation: Table 2 splits the old '216–960' idea: 46.0 from 216–230 MHz and 47.0 from 230–960 MHz for Class B at 3 m. The FCC Class B number in that broad range is 200 µV/m, about 46 dBµV/m, and do not swap the tables.

stem: ICES-003 Class B quasi-peak at 3 m from 30 MHz to 88 MHz is:
explanation: Table 2 lists 40.0 dBµV/m for Class B at 3 m in 30–88 MHz, and 30.0 dBµV/m at 10 m. Class A at 3 m in that band is 50.0.

stem: Which arrangement detail is a classic radiated fail?
choices: Cables bundled in a way the user will never use, so the maximum is never found
Writing down the mode of operation
explanation: Section 15.31 tells you to maximize with the controls and leads a user can reach. A pretty cable dress that hides the worst case is a failed method, not a quiet product.

stem: Emissions more than 20 dB under the Part 15 limit:
choices: Must be tabulated at every megahertz
Need not be reported unless another rule asks for them
Are reported only if they are quasi-peak
explanation: Section 15.31(o) is the reporting cut. It is not a second, tighter limit.

stem: The Class B limit of 500 µV/m at 3 m, extrapolated to 10 m at 20 dB/decade, is:
explanation: 500 × 3/10 = 150. Section 15.109(g)(2) uses that exact example for a Class B device above 1000 MHz.

stem: A horn antenna above 1 GHz is typically:
choices: Scanned from 1 m to 4 m exactly as a biconical
Kept at a fixed height or scanned over a smaller range, aimed at the product, in both polarizations
explanation: Above 1 GHz the method changes with the standard edition: boresight, shorter cables, and absorbers on the floor are the usual picture. Record the procedure you actually followed.

stem: Quasi-peak weighting depends on:
choices: Only the RMS value over 1 hour
Repetition rate, so infrequent clicks read lower than continuous noise of the same peak
explanation: That is why a click-type product can look terrible on peak and legal on quasi-peak. CISPR 14-1 exists in part to deal with discontinuous disturbances from appliances.

stem: Normalized site attenuation is the usual validation below 1 GHz. Above 1 GHz the usual check is:
explanation: CISPR 16-1-4 is the antenna and site document ICES-002 cites, and SVSWR is the established above-1 GHz site check. A room that passes NSA can still be unfit above 1 GHz.

stem: You measure 46 dBµV/m quasi-peak at 3 m at 300 MHz and the applicable limit is the ICES-003 Class B value. The margin is about:
choices: Not comparable, because 300 MHz has no limit
explanation: Table 2 Class B at 3 m from 230–960 MHz is 47.0 dBµV/m quasi-peak. 46 is about 1 dB under that limit, and it would be over a 40 dBµV/m limit, which is the wrong row.

stem: Floor absorbers above 1 GHz are there to:
choices: Kill the floor reflection so the site can meet the above-1 GHz validation
Increase the quasi-peak reading on purpose
explanation: Above 1 GHz the ground bounce dominates unless it is absorbed. Leaving the ferrite tiles in the closet is a common reason an SVSWR check fails.

stem: The report should state:
choices: The paint code of the chamber
Distance, detector, bandwidth, antenna, polarization, height, azimuth, and the mode that was maximized
explanation: A result without the setup cannot be repeated or compared with the limit's conditions. ICES-003 also wants the chosen method, CISPR 32 or ANSI C63.4, written down.

stem: A Class A device is measured at 3 m and the lab applies 20 dB/decade back to 10 m. A 60 dBµV/m reading at 3 m becomes about:
explanation: Moving from 3 m to 10 m lowers the field by about 10.5 dB. 60 − 10.5 is about 49.5, which rounds to the 50 dBµV/m choice here, and adding the factor instead of subtracting it invents a failure.

stem: Near-field measurements above 30 MHz are:
choices: Avoided unless the device itself makes them the right method
Required at 3 m for every product
Forbidden by the inverse-distance rule even when the standard uses 3 m
explanation: Section 15.31(f)(1) says not to measure in the near field except where the device makes that appropriate. The 3 m and 10 m distances in the rules are still the distances you extrapolate to.

stem: Both horizontal and vertical data are kept because:
choices: The higher of the two is the one that can fail the limit
The average of the two is the limit
explanation: Polarization is not optional. The maximum of the two, at the worst height and angle, is the compliance number.

stem: A bilog or hybrid antenna is typically:
choices: A prescan tool covering a wide band, with final measurements often repeated on the antenna the method names
explanation: Hybrids are convenient and have their own antenna factors. If the method calls for a biconical and a log-periodic, a hybrid prescan does not retire that requirement.

stem: ICES-003 forbids mixing, on one product:
explanation: Section 3.1 says every required measurement uses one of the two specifications, not a blend. The limit numbers stay the ICES-003 tables either way.

stem: If a spur is within a few dB of the limit on peak, the next step is:
choices: Remeasure that frequency with the detector the limit is written in
Average the spur with the ambient
explanation: The limit's detector is the one that passes or fails. Peak is a search tool below 1 GHz and a real limit, together with average, above 1 GHz.

stem: Cable loss that is left out of the calculation:
choices: Makes the reported field too high
Is removed by the quasi-peak detector
Makes the reported field too low
explanation: Uncorrected cable loss means the receiver saw less than the antenna delivered. The product looks quieter than it is.

stem: An unterminated receive cable or a loose connector usually:
choices: Raises the noise floor or adds unstable spurs
Is the preferred above-1 GHz method
explanation: A bad RF path is a measurement defect. Wiggle the connectors before you write a noncompliance.

stem: Section 15.109(g) lets digital devices use CISPR 22 Third Edition, but above 1 GHz:
explanation: The alternative does not replace the above-1 GHz Part 15 limit. The familiar example is 150 µV/m at 10 m for Class B, extrapolated from 500 µV/m at 3 m.

stem: The system to be maximized includes:
choices: The product, the support equipment needed to exercise it, and the cables between them
The product with every port empty, even ports the user will connect
A bare PCB with no enclosure, if an enclosure is what is sold
explanation: Sections 15.31(i) and (j) want a representative, exercised configuration. Empty ports that are used in real life are not a compliance configuration.

stem: A passing RE report is a comparison of:
choices: The maximized reading, in the limit's detector and at the limit's distance, against the limit
explanation: Distance, detector, and a real maximum are the three things that make the comparison mean something. Change any one of them and you are quoting a different test.

stem: Common RE fail: the receive antenna is:
choices: Set to the polarization the method asks for
Left at one height while the product's vertical pattern peaks elsewhere
explanation: Height scan exists because the ground reflection moves the lobe. One height is a sample, not a maximum.

stem: Below 30 MHz, extrapolating a 3 m reading to 30 m with 40 dB/decade divides the field by:
explanation: Forty decibels per decade is inverse distance squared. A factor of ten in distance is a factor of 100 in field strength, which is 40 dB.

stem: Access BPL below 30 MHz is the exception that uses:
choices: 40 dB/decade together with the slant-range distance, not the ordinary §15.31(f) paragraph
explanation: Section 15.31(f)(2) says its ordinary rule does not apply to Access BPL. Paragraph (f)(3) gives BPL its own 40 dB/decade slant-range method.

stem: You do not treat a standards preview as:
choices: A clue to the product family and the test list
A reason to go buy the standard
explanation: The IEC 61000-6-3 and CISPR 14 uploads in this pack are previews. Quote a number only when you have the table it came from.

stem: CISPR 14-1's contents, in the preview, include magnetic-field measurements:
choices: Only on the AC mains with a LISN
explanation: The preview contents list radiated magnetic field strength from 9 kHz to 30 MHz for that appliance standard. The limit values themselves are not in the preview.

stem: A 54 dBµV/m average limit with a 74 dBµV/m peak limit, at 3 m above 1 GHz, is:
choices: The ICES-003 Class B pair in Table 4
explanation: Table 4 Class B is 54 average and 74 peak, which is the same 20 dB peak allowance §15.35(b) describes. Class A is 60 and 80.

stem: When the standard gives both a 3 m limit and a 10 m limit, you:
choices: Use the limit written for the distance you actually measured, or extrapolate only if that standard allows it
explanation: ICES-002 Table 4 already prints both distances. Inventing a second extrapolation on top of a limit that was written for your distance double-counts the path loss.

stem: The turntable's job is to:
choices: Keep the product facing the door for the photo
Present the worst azimuth to the antenna
explanation: Azimuth search is part of finding the maximum. A fixed heading is only acceptable when the method says the product cannot be rotated and you have another way to cover the angles.

stem: A reading taken with the wrong RBW above 1 GHz:
choices: Is not comparable to a limit written for a bandwidth of at least 1 MHz
Can be corrected by the quasi-peak detector
Should be reported as average anyway
Is fine if the antenna was calibrated
explanation: Section 15.35(b) and ICES-003 Table 4 note ii both want at least 1 MHz. A 100 kHz bandwidth will under-read broadband noise.

stem: Class A at 10 m from 216–960 MHz under §15.109(b) is:
explanation: The Class A 10 m table is 90, 150, 210, and 300 µV/m. The 200 µV/m figure is the Class B 3 m limit in that same broad band, and it is the wrong cell.

stem: Before you fail a product for a single spur, check:
choices: Only the font on the plot
Antenna factor, cable loss, preamp linearity, ambient, and that the spur is still there with the product off
explanation: A noncompliance that disappears when the product is powered down is an ambient. One that moves when you touch a connector is the setup.

stem: Radiated emissions and conducted emissions answer different questions:
choices: They are the same test with the lights off
Radiated replaces the LISN below 30 MHz
One is a field at a distance; the other is a voltage on a port
explanation: A quiet LISN scan does not prove the chamber scan, or the other way around. Ports and the enclosure are different coupling paths.

stem: The preview of IEC 61000-6-3 says the highest frequency of the radiated measurement depends on:
choices: A fixed 18 GHz for every product
The EUT's highest internal frequency, in its Table 2
explanation: The contents list Table 2 for that highest frequency. The preview does not include the numeric rows, so this quiz does not invent them.

stem: 200 µV/m is approximately:
explanation: 20·log10(200) is 46.0 dBµV/m. That is the Class B §15.109 limit from 216–960 MHz at 3 m, expressed in decibels.

stem: A failure that is fixed by moving one cable 10 cm is evidence that:
choices: The maximum had not been found yet, or the pass was arrangement-dependent and must be controlled in the installation
explanation: Section 15.31(g) and §15.27 exist because cable dress changes the result. If compliance needs a particular cable, that cable has to be what the user receives or what the installer is told to fit.

stem: A maximized Class B reading of 120 µV/m at 3 m at 50 MHz versus §15.109(a) is a:
explanation: The Class B limit at 3 m in that part of the table is 100 µV/m. 120 µV/m is over it, and above 1 GHz remember the limit is an average limit.

stem: A maximized Class B reading of 170 µV/m at 3 m at 100 MHz versus §15.109(a) is a:
explanation: The Class B limit at 3 m in that part of the table is 150 µV/m. 170 µV/m is over it, and above 1 GHz remember the limit is an average limit.

stem: A maximized Class B reading of 220 µV/m at 3 m at 400 MHz versus §15.109(a) is a:
explanation: The Class B limit at 3 m in that part of the table is 200 µV/m. 220 µV/m is over it, and above 1 GHz remember the limit is an average limit.

stem: A maximized Class B reading of 520 µV/m at 3 m at 1.5 GHz versus §15.109(a) is a:
explanation: The Class B limit at 3 m in that part of the table is 500 µV/m. 520 µV/m is over it, and above 1 GHz remember the limit is an average limit.

stem: A radiated-emissions limit can be compared to a reading taken at a different distance with no extrapolation.
explanation: The limit is written at a distance. Section 15.31(f) tells you how to move a reading, and some tables already print both distances so you should not invent a third correction.

stem: Vertical polarization alone is enough for a final RE result below 1 GHz.
explanation: Both polarizations are part of finding the maximum. The higher of the two is the one that faces the limit.

stem: The IEC 61000-6-3 file in this pack is the full standard, including every limit number.
explanation: It is a preview. The contents list the tables, and the numeric rows are not in the upload, so they are not quizzed as if they were.

stem: ICES-003 Table 2 and the FCC §15.109 Class B table are the same numbers in every band.
explanation: They are close and they are not identical. ICES-003 Class B at 3 m is 47.0 dBµV/m from 230–960 MHz, while §15.109(a) is 200 µV/m, about 46 dBµV/m, from 216–960 MHz.

stem: Above 1 GHz a resolution bandwidth of 100 kHz satisfies the Part 15 minimum.
explanation: Section 15.35(b) requires at least 1 MHz unless a rule says otherwise. ICES-003 Table 4 carries the same minimum.

stem: Leaving the antenna factor out of the calculation is a valid way to gain margin.
explanation: The factor is part of the field strength. Omitting it reports a voltage, not the quantity the limit is written in.

stem: CISPR 14-1, as described by its preview, is the ITE standard used for computers.
explanation: The preview's title is household appliances, electric tools, and similar apparatus. ITE in Canada is ICES-003, which points at CISPR 32 or ANSI C63.4.
